editions.text: Yesterday registered 232 feeder visits and 16 species, a sharp increase from the recent weekly average of 63.6 visits and 10.0 species. The station’s activity ramped up following the installation of a new seed feeder on the morning of September 13, which replaced a unit that had been causing detection issues. This hardware change aligns with the steady rise in visual traffic observed over the last two days, culminating in yesterday’s high volume of Tufted Titmouse and Carolina Chickadee interactions.

The Carolina Wren was singing loudly by 06:00, well before the light reached the yard. At 07:08, just as the sun broke the horizon, the first Tufted Titmouse landed on the new feeder. By 10:30, the station recorded 205 visits, a sharp jump from the 61.3 average for this time of day.

Tufted Titmice and Carolina Chickadees dominated the early hours, with the titmice accounting for 75 of the visual visits. A Black-capped Chickadee appeared at 07:41, marking the station’s first confident record of the species. Meanwhile, a cluster of American Crows visited between 07:47 and 07:54.

Activity continued through the late morning. Northern Cardinals and Mourning Doves joined the mix, while a Ruby-throated Hummingbird made two confirmed visits. The day’s activity stands at 16 species, significantly higher than the recent weekly average of 10.3.

The total visit count reaches 227 by 15:30, significantly exceeding the recent weekly average of 83.1 visits. Northern Cardinals increase their presence in the latest hour, joining the continuing activity of Tufted Titmice and Carolina Chickadees.

A single Gray Catbird perches on a gravel surface nearby. The weather is mild with no precipitation.

The day’s total of 268 visits and twenty species confirms the surge seen in earlier editions, nearly triple the recent weekly average. The station’s high volume of Tufted Titmice and Carolina Chickadees activity continued through the afternoon, with the titmice maintaining their early dominance despite the arrival of Mourning Doves and House Finches.

As the light faded, the chorus shifted to a final burst of Northern Cardinals and Blue Jays in the last hour. A Common Gallinule was heard near the end of the day, adding to the twenty species recorded. The feeder settled as a Carolina Chickadee made the last visual contact well before sunset.

Two firsts closed the log: a Black-capped Chickadee and a Common Gallinule, both absent from the regional list for this time of year. The station ends the day with a quiet rhythm, the usual residents having filled the hours since sunrise.
